title: Strip 27 mm of insulation off a 35 mm² cable end with a round-cable stripping knife
instruction: Strip 27 mm of insulation off the free end of the cable with the cable knife, without nicking the strands.
context: Every conductor is stripped to length before it is terminated, so stripping is regular work for electricians (about 821,000 US jobs in 2025 per BLS, wire strippers among their everyday tools; O*NET: "Connect wires to circuit breakers, transformers, or other components"). Feeders, sub-mains and earthing conductors of 16 mm² and more are past stripping pliers (they stop at 16 mm²), so electricians strip them with a cable knife, here a JOKARI No. 27 SECURA, by its maker's steps: set the blade's depth, press it on, cut round, cut along to the end, peel the cut piece off. The blade must stop short of the strands: a nicked strand weakens the termination. Too short a strip and the 25 mm ferrule is not filled; too long and bare copper shows.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them (left positive). (1) A beech gauge block 150 x 50 mm and 16.5 mm tall, its long axis 60 degrees left of straight ahead, with a 12 mm hole 12.5 mm deep (its floor 4 mm above the table) whose axis is 30 cm forward and 7 cm left of the centre line, 25 mm from the block's front end. Two beech guide strips 17 x 5 mm, 6 mm high, are glued on its top along that axis, 25 mm apart, 19 to 36 mm behind the hole's axis: the knife's 22 mm body lies between them. On the hole's far side from the knife a backstop, a 90-degree V of two 10 x 3 mm steel flat bars, stands 22 mm above its top, faces 6 mm from the hole's axis. (2) A 10 cm offcut of single-core cable, H07V-K 1 x 35 mm2 (a class 5 flexible copper conductor 7.9 mm across under PVC insulation 1.2 mm thick nominal, 0.98 mm at its thinnest by IEC 60227-1; 10.3 mm across overall; 340 g per metre), cut square at both ends, 34.0 g. A reusable grip sleeve is clamped on its top 30 mm: 16 mm square 6061 aluminium bar cut 30 mm long, bored 12 mm through, with an M4 x 6 set screw (ISO 4026) in a tapped hole at mid-length, edges deburred, 11.6 g; its flats face 45 degrees to the table's edges. For each trial a fresh offcut is cut from the reel with a cable cutter, pushed into the sleeve flush with its top and the set screw tightened with a 2 mm hex key, in under a minute. The cable stands upright on its free end in the block's hole (0.85 mm of clearance all round). (3) A round-cable stripping knife, JOKARI No. 27 SECURA (part 10270; for round cables 8 to 28 mm across; 132 mm long, 29 mm wide, 35 mm high over its bracket, 72 g; a polyamide body with the blade in its front face, and a hardened band-steel bracket that closes a loop about 29 x 30 mm in front of the face). Its blade is set with the depth screw to stand 0.9 mm out of the face (checked with a caliper's depth rod), under the insulation's 0.98 mm minimum, so it cannot reach the strands. It lies on its side on the table (its 29 mm width upright), the middle of its front face 39 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, pointing 60 degrees left of straight ahead. Lying on the block with the cable through its loop, the knife has its blade 27 mm above the hole's floor (14.5 mm above the block's top), so the block sets the strip length. The knife's user guide gives the method: "Press tool against cable"; "Rotate to execute one or two circular cuts"; "Pull tool in direction of arrow to execute a longitudonal cut"; "Peel off the sheathing". The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Pressed on: the knife's loop round the cable, its face pushing the cable with at least 4.5 N (the PVC's push back on the blade's 0.4 x 0.9 mm leading edge at its 12.5 N/mm2 flow stress) and its blade on the cable's insulated end (the cable's axis within 3 mm of the blade's middle). Cut round: the cable turned at least 360 degrees against the pressed knife (or the knife round it) at one place along it (within 1.5 mm); that place's distance from the cable's end is the strip length. Cut along: the pressed knife then travels along the cable (the cable drawn through it, or the knife drawn along it) from the cut round to within 1 mm of the end. Peeled off: once cut round and cut along, the cut piece is pulled off the strands (2 N) by its own length plus 2 mm; before both cuts it stays on. Nicked: the blade's edge ever deeper into the cable than 0.98 mm, the insulation's thinnest (its set depth, less any gap between the knife's face and the cable and the cable's curve beside the blade). 1.0: peeled off with a strip of 25 to 29 mm (a 35 mm2 ferrule's 25 mm sleeve to its 29 mm maximum stripping length), not nicked; 0.5: peeled off at another length, or cut round 25 to 29 mm from the end but not peeled off; 0.25: the cable turned at least 90 degrees against the pressed knife at some point; else 0.0. A nicked conductor scores at most 0.25. In a real trial the stripped length is measured with a ruler or a caliper from the conductor's end to the insulation's cut edge (25 to 29 mm for 1.0); peeled off means the cut piece is off the conductor (photograph); after the trial the bare copper is inspected all round under a 10x loupe and each cut, nicked or flattened strand counted, the strand ends at the conductor's end are counted on a 10x photo against the count on a fresh offcut from the same reel (a class 5 35 mm2 conductor has about 276 wires of 0.40 mm), and the removed piece is looked through for strands: full credit needs no damaged or missing strand, and any caps the score at 0.25; cut round but not peeled off means the cut piece comes off by hand after the trial; the part-way cut is judged from the trial video. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the cable and the knife still for 1 s.
reset_notes: Inspect the stripped copper under the loupe, take the cut piece away, loosen the grip sleeve's set screw (2 mm hex key) and slide it off. Cut a fresh 10 cm offcut from the reel with a cable cutter (both ends square), push it into the sleeve flush with its top and tighten the screw; stand it on its free end in the gauge block's hole, flats at 45 degrees. Lay the knife back on its side in its place and check its blade still stands 0.9 mm out of the face (caliper depth rod; reset with the red screw). Under 2 minutes.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz) at real size and mass; the cable is stiff, the knife boxes at the maker's dimensions. The blade is not a collider: cut rules. Knife pressed on with at least 4.5 N (contact force): each new degree the cable turns against it is resisted by 0.045 N m (360 degrees cut it round); each new 0.5 mm it travels along is resisted by 9.6 N (cuts along). The insulated end is a hidden sleeve held fast until both cuts, then free to slide off against 2 N.
